{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Kōmura's theorem''' is a result on the [[derivative|differentiability]] of [[absolute continuity|absolutely continuous]] [[Banach space]]-valued functions, and is a substantial generalization of Lebesgue's theorem on the differentiability of the [[indefinite integral]], which is that Φ&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;''T'']&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' given by

:<math>\Phi(t) = \int_{0}^{t} \varphi(s) \, \mathrm{d} s,</math>

is differentiable at ''t'' for [[almost everywhere|almost every]] 0&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;''T'' when ''φ''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;''T'']&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' lies in the [[Lp space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup> space]] ''L''<sup>1</sup>([0,&nbsp;''T''];&nbsp;'''R''').

==Statement==
Let (''X'',&nbsp;||&nbsp;||) be a [[reflexive space|reflexive]] Banach space and let ''φ''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;''T'']&nbsp;→&nbsp;''X'' be absolutely continuous. Then ''φ'' is (strongly) differentiable almost everywhere, the derivative ''φ''&prime; lies in the [[Bochner space]] ''L''<sup>1</sup>([0,&nbsp;''T''];&nbsp;''X''), and, for all 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''T'',

:<math>\varphi(t) = \varphi(0) + \int_{0}^{t} \varphi'(s) \, \mathrm{d} s.</math>
